rows.label: Concept
rows.text: The triangle, parallelogram and polygon laws are the graphical and analytical foundations of vector addition. All three lead to the master resultant formula $R = \sqrt{P^2+Q^2+2PQ\cos\theta}$ with direction $\alpha = \tan^{-1}(Q\sin\theta/(P+Q\cos\theta))$. Special cases ($0°$, $90°$, $180°$, equal vectors, 120°) cover most NEB numericals, while equilibrium problems use the closed polygon and Lami's theorem.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Master formula: $R = \sqrt{P^2 + Q^2 + 2PQ\cos\theta}$
Direction: $\alpha = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{Q\sin\theta}{P + Q\cos\theta}\right)$ from $\vec{P}$
Equal vectors: $R = 2P\cos(\theta/2)$; $R = P$ when $\theta = 120°$

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: ❌ 'The triangle law and parallelogram law give different resultants.' ✅ They are mathematically EQUIVALENT — the triangle is half the parallelogram, so the same diagonal/resultant appears in both.  ·  ❌ Measuring the angle between the two sides INSIDE the parallelogram. ✅ $\theta$ is the angle between the vectors placed TAIL-TO-TAIL at the common origin — not the parallelogram's obtuse interior angle.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Note 1: Always draw the vectors tail-to-tail when using the parallelogram law — the wrong angle is the #1 exam error.  ·  Note 2: Memorise the three equilibrium fingerprints: closed polygon, three equal forces at 120°, and Lami's theorem.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Example 1 (Pythagoras case): a boat is rowed at 4 m/s across a river flowing at 3 m/s — resultant speed $= \sqrt{4^2+3^2} = 5$ m/s at $\tan^{-1}(3/4) \approx 36.9°$ from the boat's heading.  ·  Example 2 (equal vectors): two ropes each pull with 200 N at 60° apart — resultant $= 2(200)\cos30° = 346$ N along the bisector; this is why wide angles waste pulling force.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Covers only: triangle, parallelogram, polygon laws of vectors (within Vectors).  ·  Out of scope here: topics of neighbouring units in Physics — don't mix them.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Task 1: Derive the parallelogram law in writing (figure + perpendicular + Pythagoras + direction) without notes.  ·  Task 2: Solve 10 numericals mixing the master formula with its special cases.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Trick 1: 'Resultant equals either vector' + 'equal vectors' ⇒ angle 120° instantly.  ·  Trick 2: For max/min resultant MCQs: $R_{max} = P+Q$ at 0°, $R_{min} = |P-Q|$ at 180°.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Q1. State the triangle law of vector addition and derive $R = \sqrt{P^2+Q^2+2PQ\cos\theta}$.  ·  Q2. Show that the parallelogram law and the triangle law are equivalent.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Exam Tip 1: The parallelogram-law derivation (with figure, perpendicular drop, and the $\sin^2+\cos^2=1$ step) is a guaranteed derivation question — rehearse it in full written form.  ·  Exam Tip 2: Numericals often combine resolution with the polygon law: resolve first, add components, only then quote $R$ and $\alpha$.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Concept 1: Triangle law — head-to-tail addition; resultant is the closing vector.  ·  Concept 2: Parallelogram law — diagonal through the common origin; analytically identical to the triangle law.  ·  Concept 3: Polygon law — generalisation to any number of coplanar vectors; closure ⇒ equilibrium.  ·  Concept 4: Resultant formula and its special cases ($0°$, $90°$, $180°$, equal vectors, 120°).

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Triangle, parallelogram and polygon laws are three views of the same addition rule — use whichever suits the number of vectors.  ·  The cross-term $2PQ\cos\theta$ is what makes vector addition different from ordinary addition.  ·  A closed polygon of vectors ⇒ zero resultant ⇒ equilibrium.  ·  Lami's theorem works only for three concurrent forces in equilibrium.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: The parallelogram of forces was stated by Isaac Newton in the *Principia* (1687); Simon Stevin had already used the triangle of forces for inclined-plane problems a century earlier.  ·  Surveyors' 'traverse closure' is the polygon law in action: after measuring a circuit of angles and distances, the failure of the final polygon to close (closure error) quantifies the survey's accuracy.

rows.text: Q3. Two forces of 7 N and 5 N act at 60°. Find the magnitude and direction of the resultant.  ·  Q4. State Lami's theorem and use it to find the tensions in two strings supporting a 50 N weight at 45° each.  ·  state + explain the main idea of "Triangle, parallelogram and polygon laws of vectors" with one example.

rows.label: More hints
rows.text: Exam Tip 3: In 'show that the system is in equilibrium' questions, demonstrate the closed polygon OR both component sums equal to zero.  ·  Exam Tip 4: Always state the direction of the resultant (angle with a named vector) — magnitude alone loses a mark.

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: Example 3 (equilibrium): a picture hung on a nail by two strings — each string tension found via the triangle of forces; as the strings become horizontal, tension grows without limit ($T = W/2\cos\theta$).  ·  Example 4 (120° result): three equal forces F acting at 120° around a point give zero resultant — the geometry behind symmetric three-leg stands and tripod stability.

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: Two equal vectors have a resultant equal to either vector. The angle between them is: → C  ·  The magnitude of the resultant of two forces P and Q is ALWAYS: → B

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Scalars and vectors:** a scalar has only magnitude (mass, time, speed, energy, temperature); a vector has magnitude AND direction (displacement, velocity, force, momentum, electric field). Vectors are written $\vec{A}$ or bold **A**, with magnitude $|\vec{A}| = A$.  ·  **The three addition laws** answer one question — 'what is the single vector that has the same effect as several together?' (1) **Triangle law** (two vectors): place them head-to-tail; the resultant runs from the free tail to the free head. (2) **Parallelogram law** (two vectors from one point): draw both from a common origin; the diagonal through that origin is the resultant.…  ·  **The master formula** (obtained from either the triangle or parallelogram derivation): $R = \sqrt{P^2 + Q^2 + 2PQ\cos\theta}$ with direction $\alpha = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{Q\sin\theta}{P + Q\cos\theta}\right)$ from $\vec{P}$. Every special case follows from it.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Lami's theorem (equilibrium of 3 concurrent forces): $\frac{F_1}{\sin\alpha} = \frac{F_2}{\sin\beta} = \frac{F_3}{\sin\gamma}$  ·  Equilibrant: $\vec{E} = -\vec{R}$  ·  a·b = a₁b₁+a₂b₂+a₃b₃

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: |a×b| = |a||b|sinθ  ·  |a| = √(a²+b²+c²)  ·  The equilibrant equals the resultant in magnitude but points the opposite way.
